7 production lessons from a vector index rebuild gone sideways
A hard-earned playbook for rebuilding ANN indexes (HNSW/IVF/ScaNN, pgvector, OpenSearch, Milvus, Pinecone - pick your poison) without torching relevance, latency, or trust.
7 real production lessons from a failed vector index rebuild - cut latency, avoid drift, plan rollbacks, and ship safer ANN migrations.
Let’s be real: rebuilding a vector index should be boring.
You hit “rebuild,” you wait, you flip traffic, and your semantic search quietly gets better. That’s the dream. In reality, a rebuild is one of those operations that looks like “maintenance” until it becomes an outage, a relevance cliff, and a long weekend of “why are users searching less?”
This is a story about a rebuild that went sideways - and seven lessons that stuck.
The setup: a “simple” rebuild that turned into a production incident
We had a retrieval layer powering search and “recommended for you.” Embeddings came from a stable model, documents were chunked, and the vector store used an ANN index (HNSW in our case, but the patterns apply broadly).
We needed to rebuild because:
•
we’d changed chunking rules (fewer tiny fragments, more semantically coherent chunks),
•
we wanted to tune ANN parameters to cut p95 latency,
•
we were cleaning up old vectors that should’ve been deleted months ago.
We did the obvious thing: spin a new index, backfill, then swap.
And then:
•
p95 latency spiked (CPU pegged, memory churn, cache misses),
•
recall dropped in certain query segments (especially “long tail” product names),
•
some users saw “yesterday’s” results for a few hours,
•
the API didn’t go down, but the experience did - which is often worse.
The root cause wasn’t a single bug. It was a stack of small assumptions.
Architecture flow (what we thought we were doing)
Here’s the rebuild shape most teams aim for:
┌────────────────┐ Events ───▶ │ Chunk + Embed │ ───▶ Vectors ───▶ ┌───────────────┐ (upserts/ └────────────────┘ │ Shadow Index │ deletes) │ (new) │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────▶ └───────────────┘ │ dual-write │ │ ┌──────────────┐ └────────────────────────────────────▶ │ Live Index │ │ (old) │ └──────────────┘ Queries ───▶ Router (flags/segment) ───▶ Shadow read (sample) + Live read │ └──▶ compare metrics + relevance checks
What we actually did looked more like: “build shadow index fast, swap traffic fast, hope for the best.”
That hope is expensive.
Lesson 1: Treat index rebuilds like schema migrations, not maintenance jobs
Vector indexes aren’t just storage - they’re behavior. Change the index type, parameters, sharding, quantization, or chunking, and you change what “relevant” means under pressure.
What went wrong: We scoped the rebuild like a data task (“backfill vectors”). But the impact was product-level (“search feels worse”).
What to do instead:
•
Write a migration doc with success criteria: p95 latency, recall@k proxy metrics, CTR, “zero results” rate, etc.
•
Define blast radius: which endpoints, which users, which regions.
•
Require an explicit rollback plan before you start.
If your rebuild plan can’t answer “How do we undo this in 5 minutes?” you’re not ready.
Lesson 2: Dual-write is necessary, but it’s not sufficient
Dual-write is the comforting checkbox: “We write to old and new indexes so they stay in sync.”
Cool. But dual-write has sharp edges.
What went wrong: Deletes were inconsistent. Upserts landed in both indexes, but some deletes only hit one (a queue retry path dropped delete events under load). The new index quietly accumulated ghosts.
Fix pattern:
•
Treat writes as idempotent with a canonical (doc_id, chunk_id, version) key.
•
Model deletes as first-class events, not “best effort.”
•
Add a reconciliation job that periodically compares counts/hashes.
A simple reconciliation sketch:
# Pseudocode: reconcile live vs shadow by partition def reconcile(partition_id): live = live_index.list_ids(partition_id) shadow = shadow_index.list_ids(partition_id) missing_in_shadow = live - shadow extra_in_shadow = shadow - live if missing_in_shadow: shadow_index.backfill(missing_in_shadow) if extra_in_shadow: shadow_index.delete(extra_in_shadow)
Yes, listing IDs can be expensive. Partition aggressively (time buckets, tenants, shards) and do it incrementally. The point is: prove sync, don’t assume it.
Lesson 3: Your “rebuild speed” is limited by everything you forgot to capacity plan
The rebuild hammered CPU and memory. Not because indexing is magical, but because it competes with live traffic for the same resources.
What went wrong: We backfilled at full throttle on the same cluster that served queries. Index construction fought query-time graph traversal. Cache thrash made latency worse, which increased timeouts, which triggered retries, which… you know the rest.
What changed afterwards:
•
Allocate separate build capacity (even temporary) or throttle rebuild rate.
•
Put a hard cap on concurrent index inserts.
•
Pre-calculate memory headroom for the new structure (HNSW graph links, PQ codebooks, IVF lists - whatever your engine uses).
Rule of thumb you can actually use: assume peak build load is “query load + indexing load,” not "query load replaces indexing load."
Lesson 4: “Swap traffic” is not a switch, it’s a ramp with guardrails
We flipped traffic too quickly. The index wasn’t warmed. The caches were cold. The router didn’t have enough segmentation logic.
What went wrong: After the swap, p95 latency rose sharply because the new index had zero query cache history and OS page cache hadn’t learned the working set. We saw latency spikes that looked like regressions but were actually “first day in a new apartment” chaos.
Do this instead:
•
Shadow-read a percentage of traffic first (1% → 5% → 20%).
•
Only ramp up if SLOs hold for a fixed window.
•
Warm the index with top queries and recent queries before major ramps.
If you don’t have a query replay job, that’s your homework.
Lesson 5: Relevance drift isn’t obvious until you instrument it
Here’s the sneaky part: you can keep latency stable and still ship a worse experience.
What went wrong: We tuned ANN parameters for speed (lower efSearch / fewer probes), which helped p95, but it disproportionately hurt certain query classes - especially “needle in haystack” queries and multi-intent queries.
Add a relevance harness:
•
Maintain a small but curated golden query set (50–200 queries) with expected top results or “acceptable set.”
•
Track overlap@k between live and shadow: how many results match in top 10?
•
Track behavioral proxies: “search refine” rate, “back to search” rate, time-to-click.
A practical overlap metric:
overlap@10 = |Top10(live) ∩ Top10(shadow)| / 10
Low overlap isn’t always bad (maybe shadow is better), but sudden segment drops are a red flag.
Lesson 6: Observability needs to include vector-specific signals
Traditional monitoring says “API is up” while retrieval silently degrades.
What we missed initially:
•
index build queue depth,
•
insert throughput vs expected,
•
segment-level recall proxies,
•
“empty result” rate by query type,
•
ANN-specific internal stats (visited nodes, probes, efSearch effectiveness).
What we added:
•
dashboards for p50/p95/p99, not just averages,
•
per-tenant and per-endpoint breakdowns,
•
alerting on relevance proxies, not only errors.
Because a retrieval outage often looks like: “everything returns 200 OK, just… wrong.”
Lesson 7: Rollback must be boring, fast, and rehearsed
We had a rollback path, but it wasn’t frictionless. Dependencies had already shifted. Some components assumed the new index schema. The “easy revert” turned into a careful multi-step dance.
What you want instead:
•
A router kill switch (feature flag) that forces reads to old index immediately.
•
A deployment strategy where old and new can run side-by-side without schema conflict.
•
A rollback runbook you practice once, when nobody’s panicking.
If you’ve never performed the rollback in a staging environment that resembles prod, you don’t have a rollback - you have a wish.
Closing thoughts: rebuilds are where “ML systems” become “real systems”
Vector search feels modern. Sleek. Almost magical.
But production doesn’t care about magic. It cares about failure modes, backpressure, sync guarantees, and whether your “simple rebuild” accidentally changes the meaning of relevance for paying users.
If you’re planning a rebuild soon, steal this checklist:
•
migration success metrics (latency + relevance),
•
dual-write + reconciliation,
•
isolated or throttled build capacity,
•
gradual ramp + warmup,
•
relevance harness + segment analysis,
•
vector-aware observability,
•
rollback kill switch + rehearsal.
And if you’ve lived through a rebuild disaster of your own… I want the story. Seriously - drop it in the comments. I read those. Follow for more production war stories and the boring practices that save weekends.
